caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1515, imaged by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This portrait shows NGC 1515, a galaxy that astronomers classify as an intermediate barred spiral. It lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado. The Dark Energy Camera captured it from the Blanco 4-meter Telescope, part of Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, which is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

Spiral galaxies are flattened discs of stars, gas and dust whose arms wind out from a bright centre. In a barred spiral, a straight band of stars runs across the middle, and the arms tend to begin near its ends. An intermediate type sits between the classic barred and unbarred forms, with a bar that is present but not dominant.
The data come from the Dark Energy Survey, a project that charted millions of galaxies. Surveys like this capture individual galaxies as a side benefit of their wider mapping work.
explore: The Dark Energy Camera ranks among the world's most powerful digital cameras. It was built with the Dark Energy Survey in mind, and the US Department of Energy and NSF operated it between 2013 and 2019.

understand.summary: The image combines visible-light exposures from the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope, taken through g, r and i filters. The packet does not say which display colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The camera collects light over long exposures from a large telescope, so it records a faint, distant galaxy that would be invisible to the unaided eye.

alt: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1515 as recorded by the Dark Energy Camera.

caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its companions M32 and NGC 205, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt Telescope at Kitt Peak
story: The large spiral filling this frame is M31, the Andromeda Galaxy, with two small companions: M32 below the centre and NGC 205, also called M110, towards the upper right. The view spans more than two and a quarter degrees of sky, more than four full-Moon widths, and still does not take in the whole galaxy.

Andromeda is our nearest large, normal neighbour, a spiral very much like the Milky Way and a little bigger. Seen from far away, the two would look like a pair. It is faintly visible to the naked eye, and the Persian astronomer Al-Sufi described it as a 'little cloud' as early as 964 AD.

Dark dust lanes show up against the core only on the western, right-hand side, which tells astronomers that side is tipped towards us. The galaxy's rotation also hints that there may be ten times more matter than we can see, spread through a vast dark halo.
explore: The picture began as three photographic plates taken in 1979 on the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak. Undergraduate Vanessa Harvey digitised them in the summer of 1996 with Kitt Peak's PDS scanner, as part of an NSF-funded Research Experience for Undergraduates program.
At Andromeda's heart is a tightly packed star cluster, though it is washed out in this saturated image.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image built from three digitised photographic plates, each made with a different emulsion and filter. The three frames approximate red, green and blue, giving an estimate of true colour.
understand.eye: To the unaided eye only Andromeda's bright inner bulge is visible; the long plate exposures reveal the spiral arms, dust lanes and companions.

scaleExtra: The Andromeda Galaxy is approximately 2.2 million light-years away and over 65,000 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A large, tilted spiral galaxy stretches across the frame, with a small companion galaxy below its centre and another to the upper right.

caption: The Whirlpool Galaxy, M51 (NGC 5194/5195), imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
story: This colour view shows M51, the Whirlpool: the large spiral galaxy NGC 5194 and its smaller, barred and more shapeless companion NGC 5195. The companion takes on a reddish tint because it sits behind the dusty arm that links it to the main galaxy.

M51 holds a special place in history. In 1845 the Third Earl of Rosse made out spiral structure here, the first time it had been seen in any astronomical object. Its arms are perhaps the neatest textbook example in any nearby galaxy, and such regularity suggests something keeps them in shape. The tidal pull of NGC 5195 may do it, by generating spiral density waves.

Although the Whirlpool is smaller and less massive than our own Galaxy, it is considerably brighter. That is because recent star formation has filled it with hot, luminous young stars of the O and B types.
explore: Because the system is so large on the sky, the image was made with a 'drift scan': the telescope stayed fixed while the sky moved across the detector, with each row of the chip shifted along in step. The same spiral pattern also shows up in radio emission, suggesting the galaxy's magnetic fields are squeezed by the density wave.

understand.summary: Three CCD frames from the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope, taken through filters roughly matching red, green and blue, were combined to recreate a true-colour picture. The colour balance was reworked in July 2000.
understand.eye: The combined CCD exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out colour and detail in the galaxies.

scaleExtra: M51 lies approximately 31 million light-years away and is over 65,000 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A spiral galaxy with well-defined arms, one of which connects to a smaller, reddish companion galaxy.

caption: SOAR and Gemini South beneath the Milky Way, Cerro Pachón, Chile
story: Under a dusty Milky Way and the faint glow of the upper atmosphere, two telescope domes stand on Cerro Pachón in Chile. The Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope, SOAR, is at the centre, and the International Gemini Observatory's Gemini South is on the right. A photographer at the lower left, gazing over the dry landscape, gives a sense of how big the 4.1-meter SOAR telescope is.

Behind SOAR, Gemini South is firing its laser guide star, an artificial point of light in the sky. Adaptive optics systems need a sharp reference light to measure and undo the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere, yet only a few real stars are bright enough for the job. A laser can be aimed wherever the telescope points.
On 8-meter-class telescopes such as Gemini South, this technology lets a ground-based observatory produce images as sharp as those from telescopes in space.
explore: SOAR is one of almost 40 telescopes at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. Gemini South is one half of the International Gemini Observatory. The photo comes from the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all NOIRLab sites, by Audiovisual Ambassador Tomáš Slovinský.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Cerro Pachón, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and airglow appear brighter than they would to someone standing on the mountain.

alt: Two telescope domes on a dry mountaintop under the Milky Way, with a laser beam rising from the right-hand dome and a small human figure at lower left.

caption: Collecting Globe at Night data, Saguaro National Park East, Arizona
story: In Saguaro National Park East, just outside Tucson, Arizona, Connie Walker is gathering observations for Globe at Night. This citizen science project tracks and reports how light pollution affects the visibility of the night sky, using observations sent in by the public.

Walker created the project in 2006 with Steve Pompea, now scientist emeritus at NSF NOIRLab, built around a simple web application. Over 17 years, more than 250,000 people around the world have contributed data on how visible the stars are.

Those reports have made a real scientific difference. A study published in the journal Science in January 2023 analysed the submitted observations and found that skyglow is rising faster than satellite measurements of Earth's night-time brightness had suggested.
explore: Globe at Night is one of many NOIRLab efforts to protect dark skies. In February 2022, NOIRLab and the SKA Observatory were named co-hosts of a new IAU centre that works to shield dark and quiet skies from interference by large satellite constellations.

understand.summary: This is a night-time photograph taken with a camera in Saguaro National Park East, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the scene may appear brighter here than it would have to someone standing there.

alt: Connie Walker collecting Globe at Night observations after dark in Saguaro National Park East.

caption: Star cluster NGC 6520 and dark cloud Barnard 86, imaged by Gemini South
story: A scatter of hot, massive young stars, arranged in a shape that recalls a dandelion's seed head, sits beside a dark, gecko-shaped cloud. The cluster is NGC 6520, and the cloud is Barnard 86, a Bok globule that may be the remains of the material the stars formed from.

The story began millions of years ago, when a dust cloud started to collapse and give birth to stars. The cluster is now thought to be around 200 million years old. Its stars together weigh roughly 300 to 400 times as much as the Sun, while Barnard 86 still holds enough material for about 3,000 more Sun-like stars.

Because the two lie so close together, astronomers suspect they are related. A southern sky survey that picked out hydrogen-alpha light from warm, ionised gas shows a nebula reaching from the dark globule out to embrace the cluster.
explore: The image covers a 9.7 by 5.4 arcminute patch of the crowded Sagittarius star cloud and gives the clearest optical view yet of the pair. Amateur astronomers with moderate-to-large telescopes also seek out the cluster and its dark neighbour.

understand.summary: Gemini South's GMOS instrument recorded this in four filters spanning near-ultraviolet to near-infrared light. The u-band is shown as blue, g-band as cyan, r-band as yellow and i-band as red.
understand.eye: The u and i filters reach slightly beyond the colours the eye can see, and the big telescope collects far more light, so faint stars and the dark cloud's edges show clearly.

scaleExtra: The cluster lies around 5,500 light-years from the Sun, according to Gemini Observatory.
alt: A loose cluster of bright stars beside a dark, irregular cloud set against a dense field of stars.
flags: caption gives two distances and ages

caption: Full Moon rising over Maunakea, Hawaiʻi
story: The full Moon rises over Maunakea, and beneath it a dark triangle stretches across the sky: the shadow of the volcano itself. Maunakea is a dormant volcano that hosts Gemini North, one of the two telescopes of the International Gemini Observatory, along with a number of other observatories.

The shadow's neat triangular shape is an optical effect, since the mountain is not triangular. The shadow is so long that its irregular edges blur together into a rectangle. That rectangle then tapers into the distance and seems to meet at a single point on the horizon, thanks to the curvature of the Earth and ordinary perspective.

The summit is very dry even though the island below is tropical and frequently cloudy. The climb of about 4000 meters (14,000 feet) from the Pacific Ocean to the top creates an inversion layer, which traps thick clouds below and leaves the peak above them.
explore: Those trapped clouds often hide the land and sea beneath, creating an unusual view from the mountaintop. Gemini North is operated by NSF NOIRLab, with partial backing from the U.S. National Science Foundation.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera on Maunakea, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The Moon and the volcano's shadow can be seen by eye, but a camera exposure may render the sky and colours differently from how they look in person.

alt: A full Moon rises above a dark, triangular shadow cast by the volcano.

caption: The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) and the Pelican Nebula, imaged with a 16-inch telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Glowing clouds shaped like the North American continent spread across this wide view in the constellation Cygnus. This is NGC 7000, the North America Nebula. Much of the nebulosity lies in front of the Milky Way's band, and where the dust and gas thin out, crowds of stars in that spiral arm show through.

The four-frame mosaic covers more than 4 degrees of sky, enough to fit over 30 full Moons. The very bright star at right is Deneb, but it has nothing to do with the nebula; it is well over 1,500 light-years away, while the glowing clouds are closer.

For a long time, astronomers were puzzled about which star makes the nebula shine. A paper by Fernando Comeron and Anna Pasquali, published in fall 2004, seems to have identified it. The star hides behind thick dust, and they found it by searching in infrared light for a hot, bright star.
explore: The culprit sits just off the coast of the nebula's 'Florida', in its 'Atlantic Ocean'. The image was made by Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light mosaic of four frames taken with a 16-inch RCOS telescope and CCD camera, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The nebula is far too faint and too large for the eye to see in this detail; long exposures stitched together reveal its glow and shape.

alt: A glowing cloud shaped like the North American continent spreads across a dense star field, with a very bright star at the right edge.

caption: The Milky Way and the Gum Nebula above Cerro Tololo, Chile
story: The Milky Way, speckled with stars of many colours, sweeps down towards a city-lit horizon above the telescopes of Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. It passes just by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope on the left and the SMARTS 1.5-meter Telescope on the right, and the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds appear to the left of the Blanco dome.
Between the two telescopes a deep red glow spreads among the Milky Way's tendrils. It is the Gum Nebula, an emission nebula that shines because its gas has been ionised by the stars within it.

From our point of view the nebula contains a wealth of objects, including globular clusters, the Vela Pulsar and a supernova remnant about 11,000 years old. Emission nebulae like this often glow red because hydrogen gas gives off light at that colour.
explore: Cerro Tololo is a Program of NSF NOIRLab. This photograph, by Tomáš Slovinský, was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Cerro Tololo, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the faint red nebula and star colours stand out far more than they would in person.

alt: The Milky Way descends towards a lit horizon between two observatory domes, with a red glow between them and the Magellanic Clouds to the left.

caption: Lightning above Maunaloa, Hawaiʻi
story: A bolt of lightning lights up the clouds over Maunaloa, the volcano that faces Maunakea across Hawaiʻi. A second, smaller bolt hides inside the clouds on the left side of the photograph.

Maunakea is home to Gemini North, one of the two telescopes making up the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with support in part from the U.S. National Science Foundation. For 80% of the year the summit offers superb conditions for observing the night sky, but now and then thunderstorms like this one roll through.

These storms are rare, and Gemini North and its neighbours near the summit are affected only for a while. The observatory buildings generally include structures designed to protect the telescopes from lightning strikes. Lightning itself is a giant electrical discharge inside storm clouds, and its flash briefly can light up a cloud from within.
explore: Lightning is not the only electrical display seen near Maunakea. Earlier NOIRLab Images of the Week have featured red sprites, a related lightning phenomenon, near the mountain.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera in Hawaiʻi, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: Lightning lasts only an instant for the eye, but a camera can freeze it and record the lit clouds in more detail.

alt: A bright bolt of lightning illuminates clouds over a volcano at night, with a fainter bolt in the clouds at left.

caption: The star cluster NGC 6624, imaged by Gemini Observatory with GeMS
story: This Gemini Observatory image of the star cluster NGC 6624 was made with the GeMS system, and it separates individual stars all the way into the cluster's crowded core. Normally, the heart of a dense cluster blurs into a single glow when seen from the ground, because Earth's turbulent atmosphere smears starlight.

Being able to pick out stars one by one matters because a cluster's stars are generally thought to have formed at around the same time. Measuring them carefully lets astronomers work out how old the whole group is.

The study behind this image found an age of between 11.5 and 12.5 billion years for NGC 6624. That confirms the cluster took shape when the cosmos was still young, just a fraction of its present age, which is about 13.8 billion years. Old clusters like this preserve stars that formed when the Universe was young.
explore: The composite colour image was produced by Travis Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage.

understand.summary: The image was taken at Gemini Observatory with the GeMS system and assembled as a colour composite. The packet does not list the filters or say what the colours represent.
understand.eye: No eye could separate these tightly packed stars; the telescope and its sharp-focus system resolve them individually.

alt: A dense star cluster whose individual stars are resolved right into its crowded centre.

caption: The interacting galaxy trio LGG 455 (NGC 7232, NGC 7233 and NGC 7232B), imaged by Gemini South
story: Three galaxies share this view: NGC 7232 at upper right, NGC 7233 at lower right and NGC 7232B on the left. Together they form an interacting trio called Lyon Group of Galaxies #455, or LGG 455. The two brightest points near the centre are not galaxies at all, but foreground stars in our own Milky Way.
Dark lanes of dust cross NGC 7232 and NGC 7233, while NGC 7232B has bright spots of young, blue stars scattered along its weak spiral arms.

Little detailed research has been done on the group, but it is thought to contain a rare 'dark galaxy': a cloud holding the raw ingredients for stars that has never managed to form any. Its gas could make more than 400 million Suns, yet this deep Gemini image finds no significant population of stars there, just left of the lower foreground star.
explore: Most likely, that gas was thrown out of NGC 7233 when it passed close to one of the other two galaxies. Ryan Soares suggested this field for the Australian/Gemini Student Imaging Contest, and Travis Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage produced the colour composite.

understand.summary: The data were taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini South in Chile, in visible and near-infrared light through g, r and i filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye; a large telescope collecting light over long exposures reveals their dust lanes and young stars.

alt: Two galaxies with dark dust lanes on the right and a spiral with blue spots on the left, with two bright foreground stars near the centre.

caption: The Milky Way over Maunakea, with Mauna Loa in the distance, Hawaiʻi
story: The Milky Way's starry band hangs overhead in this panorama from Maunakea, home of Gemini North. On the mountain at the centre, a winding ribbon of light traces an access road. Far below, the large towns of the Island of Hawaiʻi glow in patches beneath the clouds, and the active volcano Mauna Loa rises above them.

Maunakea and Mauna Loa are both shield volcanoes, the broad, gently sloping kind built up by many flows of runny lava. The difference is that Maunakea is dormant, which is fortunate for the observatories on its summit.

The mountain's volcanic past still helps astronomers today. Its smooth, sloping sides and great height are two of the reasons the summit enjoys exceptional observing conditions. A high peak places telescopes above much of the atmosphere's moisture and turbulence.
explore: Gemini North is one half of the International Gemini Observatory. It is operated by NSF NOIRLab, with support in part from the U.S. National Science Foundation.

understand.summary: This is a panoramic landscape photograph taken with a camera on Maunakea, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed than it would to someone on the summit.

alt: A panorama of the Milky Way above a dark mountain with a winding lit road, and a distant volcano rising above clouds lit by towns.

caption: The Cygnus X-1 black hole system and its jet bowshock, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Near the centre of this wide view sit two stars; the brighter, lower one is Cygnus X-1. It looks like a single star, but it is actually a binary system that contains a black hole. Above it, at top centre, curves a bluish shape like an umbrella, and bright orange gas spreads along the left side.

In Cygnus X-1, the black hole pulls gas away from its companion star. Before the gas falls in, it grows so hot that it gives off X-rays, which is how the system was discovered. Not all of it is swallowed: some is launched outwards in jets of hot gas.

The jet itself can't be seen here, but its effect can. The bluish umbrella is a bowshock, formed where gas in the jet slams into gas in the surrounding nebula. The orange glow on the left belongs to Sharpless 101, an emission nebula whose western edge reaches into the frame.
explore: Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope took the image using its wide-field Mosaic camera. North is up and east is to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope recorded light from specific glowing gases. According to the caption, hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulphur [S II] in blue, though the packet's filter table lists oxygen [O III] and hydrogen-alpha filters.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate light from individual gases, so faint structures like the bowshock stand out in a way the eye could never see.

alt: A star field with a bluish umbrella-shaped arc at top centre, two stars near the middle, and orange glowing gas along the left side.

caption: The Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24) with IC 1284 and NGC 6590, imaged with a 16-inch telescope at Kitt Peak
story: A large oval crowd of bluish stars stands out towards the right of this picture. This is M24, the Sagittarius Star Cloud. Also near the right side, IC 1284 shines a vivid red, while NGC 6590 spreads a bluish haze around a handful of bright stars.

Our galaxy, as this view shows, is always partly cloudy. Just as clouds on Earth can hide part of a starry sky, vast clouds of gas and dust block whatever lies behind them. Yet there are gaps, even towards the densest regions of the Milky Way.

Looking at M24, a grouping of young, bright stars, means peering through one such gap to regions much deeper, towards an inner spiral arm. In the northern part of the star cloud, several dark nebulae provide contrast against the countless background stars. Red glows usually come from hydrogen gas, while blue haze is typically starlight scattered by dust.
explore: The image was made by Fred Calvert and Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a 16-inch RCOS telescope and CCD camera using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing faint red and blue nebulae and dark clouds that would be hard to see even through a telescope.

scaleExtra: The stars of M24 are many thousands of light-years away, perhaps about 10,000, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A dense field of stars with a large oval cluster of bluish stars on the right, a red glowing patch and a bluish haze around bright stars, crossed by dark clouds.

caption: Pickering's Triangle in the Cygnus Loop, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This wide-field view shows Pickering's Triangle, part of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan. The same remnant includes the well-known Veil Nebula.

A supernova remnant is the expanding debris of a star that exploded, sweeping up and heating the gas around it until it glows. Astronomers estimate that the explosion behind this one happened somewhere between 5,000 and 10,000 years ago. Its whole shell now stretches across more than six full Moons on the sky.

To capture it, Travis Rector and Heidi Schweiker combined two full pointings of the 64-megapixel NOAO Mosaic-1 camera, which sits on the historic Mayall 4-meter telescope, an NSF facility at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The result is a double-wide image that shows a larger slice of the remnant.
explore: The picture was unveiled in Austin, Texas, during the American Astronomical Society's 211th meeting and featured in an NOAO press release.

understand.summary: The Mosaic-1 camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used narrowband filters that isolate light from oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen gas. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The remnant is too faint to see by eye; narrow filters and long exposures bring out its glowing gas.

scaleExtra: Pickering's Triangle is about 1,500 light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A wide-field view of Pickering's Triangle, part of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant, among stars.

caption: The Dumbbell Nebula (M27), imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: The Dumbbell Nebula, M27, is a bubble of gas thrown off by a star near the end of its life, like others of its kind. What is left of the star's core sits at the centre, visible as a slightly bluish star just above a small triangle of white stars, and it makes the bubble glow.

Surprisingly, in visible light the gas shines more brightly than the central star. The reason is that the star emits most of its light at shorter, more energetic wavelengths such as ultraviolet, which our eyes cannot see. The surrounding gas absorbs that energy and re-emits it as visible light, so we see the bubble rather than the source.

Through a small telescope or from city skies, the brighter part of the nebula looks like a half-eaten apple core, which gave it its name. From dark Kitt Peak, and in this image, the full bubble is easy to see.
explore: The nebula's age is estimated at 3,500 years. The image was made by Joe and Gail Metcalf with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Through a small telescope the eye sees mainly the bright apple-core shape; a long camera exposure reveals the complete, fainter bubble.

scaleExtra: M27 is perhaps 1,000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A glowing bubble of gas with a brighter central region, and a slightly bluish star at its centre above a small triangle of white stars.

caption: The Little Dumbbell Nebula (M76), imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: M76, the Little Dumbbell, shows two distinct features: a bright inner rectangle and very faint outer loops. The rectangle is in fact a ring-shaped torus seen edge-on.

Like most nebulae of this type, these loops were shed as a star of average mass came to the end of its life. More massive stars explode, but this process is much gentler, and it produces the tangled bubbles seen here.

At the heart of the nebula lies a double star, and the upper one is distinctly blue. That hot star is what makes the Little Dumbbell glow, as its energetic light excites the surrounding gas. Its distance is not well known, but most estimates put it between 3000 and 5000 light-years away, which would make the bubble roughly a light-year across. On a dark night, the nebula is a rewarding sight through the 20-inch telescope at Kitt Peak.
explore: The full-resolution image shows the central double star most clearly. The picture was taken by Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Through the 20-inch telescope the eye can make out both the bright rectangle and the very dim outer loops, but the camera gathers far more of their faint light.

scaleExtra: M76 is thought to lie between 3000 and 5000 light-years away, making the bubble about a light-year across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A nebula with a bright central rectangle flanked by faint outer loops, and a small blue star at its centre.

caption: Sharpless 157 (WR 157), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This image is titled Sharpless 157 (WR 157), a nebula in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was recorded with the Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope, through narrow filters that each pick out light from one kind of glowing gas: oxygen, sulphur or hydrogen.

Objects in the Sharpless catalogue are clouds of gas that glow in visible light. In nebulae like these, hot stars flood nearby gas with energetic light, stripping electrons from its atoms. When the atoms recapture electrons, they give off light at particular colours, and each element leaves its own signature.

That is why narrow filters are so useful. By isolating each gas separately, astronomers can map where oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen are glowing and learn about the conditions inside the cloud. The official caption supplied with this image describes a different object, so no further details about this nebula are given here.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope recorded this through narrowband filters for oxygen [O III], sulphur [S II] and hydrogen-alpha light. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing structure the eye could not see.

alt: A wide-field view of the nebula Sharpless 157, recorded through narrowband filters.

caption: The planetary nebula Abell 39, imaged by the WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope
story: This picture shows Abell 39, a planetary nebula with rare and beautiful spherical symmetry, in the constellation Hercules. The name comes from its place as number 39 in George Abell's 1966 catalogue of large nebulae he had discovered.

A planetary nebula is the shell of gas cast off by a Sun-like star late in its life; the name is historical and has nothing to do with planets. Most are lopsided or complicated in shape, which is why this near-perfect sphere caught the attention of astronomers George Jacoby of WIYN Observatory, Gary Ferland of the University of Kentucky and Kirk Korista of Western Michigan University.
The team selected it for study precisely because of that unusual symmetry. The nebula measures about five light-years across, while its shell is only about a third of a light-year thick.
explore: The picture was taken in 1997 at Kitt Peak National Observatory near Tucson, using the 3.5-m (138-inch) telescope of the WIYN Observatory. It was the subject of a press release at the 197th meeting of the American Astronomical Society in January 2001.

understand.summary: The WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope took this through a single blue-green filter that isolates light emitted by oxygen atoms at 500.7 nanometers. The packet does not describe how the image was coloured.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, and the filter records only one narrow colour of light from oxygen.

alt: A round shell of gas set among stars.

caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-174, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A very blue star sits near the centre of a patch of blue gas in this wide-field view. This is Sh2-174 in the constellation Cepheus, an unusual and ancient planetary nebula.

A planetary nebula forms when a star of low mass sheds its outer layers as it dies. What remains of the star's core is a white dwarf, and normally it lies very close to the middle of the cloud it has cast off.

Sh2-174 breaks that pattern. Its white dwarf, the very blue star, is shifted off to the right rather than sitting at the centre. Astronomers put this lopsidedness down to the nebula running into the thin interstellar gas that surrounds it. A planetary nebula normally expands evenly around its star, so an off-centre white dwarf is a clue that something outside the nebula is at work.
explore: The wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope recorded the scene. In this image north is up and east is to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope combined broadband and narrowband filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange, hydrogen-alpha in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches into near-infrared light beyond the eye's range, and the narrow filters bring out faint gas the eye could not see.

alt: Clouds of gas with a very blue star near the centre of a bluish region.

caption: The Lagoon Nebula (M8), imaged with a 16-inch telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This wide view shows M8, the Lagoon Nebula, a vast region of our galaxy where stars are forming. On a dark night it is easy to spot without any optical aid, just above the spout of the 'teapot' pattern of stars in Sagittarius. Through a small telescope, a milky glow of nebulosity fills the whole field of view.

A star cluster called NGC 6530 shows how star formation is proceeding inside the cloud. A few of its stars appear at the bottom right of this picture, though most of the cluster lies just beyond the frame to the right.

CCD images such as this one hint at how turbulent the nebula's gas is. As new stars form, their strong winds and radiation heat and stir up the material they were born from, sculpting the cloud around them. Regions like the Lagoon are where stars like the Sun are thought to be born.
explore: The image was taken by Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a 16-inch RCOS telescope and CCD camera using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: By eye the Lagoon appears as a faint, milky glow; a long camera exposure brings out its colour and turbulent structure.

alt: A wide field of glowing, turbulent nebulosity with a few cluster stars at the lower right.

caption: The Whale Galaxy (NGC 4631) and NGC 4627, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: NGC 4631, known as the Whale Galaxy, is a huge spiral galaxy that we see edge-on, so its disc appears as a long, narrow band. Astronomers class it as an Sc type spiral. Next to it lies a smaller companion, NGC 4627.

The companion seems to have bent the Whale slightly out of shape. Together, the two appear as entry Arp 281 in the Arp Catalog of Peculiar galaxies, and faint tidal tails can be traced between them. Tidal tails are streams of stars and gas pulled out when galaxies tug on one another with their gravity.

The Whale has another neighbour beyond the edge of this frame, to the southeast. That galaxy, NGC 4656, looks noticeably distorted, apparently from its own encounters with NGC 4631. Detailed surveys have found a thin bridge of hydrogen gas linking the two, a sign that they interacted in the past.
explore: The image was made by John Vickery and Jim Matthes with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint features such as tidal tails that the eye could not see even through a telescope.

scaleExtra: This group of galaxies lies between 25 and 30 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A long, edge-on spiral galaxy with a small companion galaxy nearby and faint streams between them.

caption: The star cluster NGC 6520 and dust cloud Barnard 86, imaged by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Bright young stars of the open cluster NGC 6520 stand out against a crowded backdrop, with the dark dust cloud Barnard 86 nearby. The pair lies in the constellation Sagittarius, towards one of the densest parts of our Galaxy.

The background is packed with older stars from our Galaxy's central bulge. The cluster's young stars contrast with them sharply, and they probably formed out of gas connected to the neighbouring dust cloud.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Dark clouds like Barnard 86 are dense enough to block the light of the stars behind them, so they appear as shadowy shapes against the starry background. Seeing a young cluster sitting beside such a cloud offers a glimpse of where its stars may have come from.
explore: The image was taken on June 24th, 2007 with NSF's Blanco 4-m telescope at Cerro Tololo. It was released during 'Around the World in 80 Telescopes', a webcast held on April 3-4, 2009, as part of the 100 Hours of Astronomy during the International Year of Astronomy 2009.

understand.summary: The Blanco 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic II camera recorded this in visible and near-infrared light. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches beyond the colours the eye can see, and the long exposure reveals far more stars than an observer could.

alt: A group of bright stars set against a dense field of fainter stars, next to a dark cloud of dust.

caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31), imaged with a 16-inch telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This wide view shows M31, the Andromeda Galaxy, the spiral galaxy closest to our own Milky Way. It lies in the constellation Andromeda, and on a clear night without the Moon it can easily be found with the naked eye.
People have known about it for a long time. The Persian astronomer Al Sufi mentioned the galaxy in 905 A.D., and it appears on star charts made before the telescope was invented.

Its size on the sky is surprising. From a dark site away from city lights, a good pair of binoculars can trace it across about 4 degrees. For comparison, the full Moon covers only about 1/2 a degree. A spiral galaxy is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind out from a bright central bulge, and Andromeda's faint outer disc extends far beyond the glow most people notice.
explore: The image was taken by Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a 16-inch RCOS telescope and CCD camera using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: To the naked eye Andromeda is a faint smudge; long camera exposures reveal much more of its extent and structure.

scaleExtra: The Andromeda Galaxy is located 2.3 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A wide telescope view of the Andromeda Galaxy.

caption: The twisted spiral galaxy NGC 3718 and its neighbours, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: In the upper-right corner of this image is NGC 3718, a spiral galaxy with a strangely twisted shape. To its left sits a smaller spiral, NGC 3729. The distorted form of NGC 3718 is probably the result of gravitational tugging between the two.
Lower down and to the right of the twisted spiral lies a tight knot of galaxies known as Hickson Compact Group 56, made up of five galaxies that are interacting with each other.

These five look tiny next to the big twisted spiral, but that is an illusion of distance. They are not actually smaller; instead, their distance from us is roughly eight times that of the two big spirals. In a flat picture of the sky, objects at very different distances can appear side by side, and apparent size alone can be misleading.
explore: The picture comes from the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. The image is rotated 35 degrees counterclockwise from the usual orientation of north up and east left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used five filters. U is shown as violet, B as blue, V as green, I as orange and hydrogen-alpha as red.
understand.eye: The U and I filters record near-ultraviolet and near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and long exposures reveal galaxies far too faint for the eye.

alt: A twisted spiral galaxy at upper right, a smaller spiral to the left, and a compact group of small galaxies below and to the right.

caption: The Soap Bubble Nebula (PN G75.5+1.7), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A remarkably round shell floats in this image: the planetary nebula nicknamed the Soap Bubble, officially PN G75.5+1.7, in the constellation Cygnus. It lies not far from the Crescent Nebula, NGC 6888.

A planetary nebula is the shell of gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star. Most are irregular, but this shell's spherical symmetry is striking, making it very much like another planetary nebula, Abell 39.

Despite its neat shape, it was found only recently. The Soap Bubble is faint, and it sits within a larger, diffuse nebula, which together kept it hidden. Amateur astronomer Dave Jurasevich discovered it on July 6th, 2008, and Keith Quattrocchi and Mel Helm noted and reported it on July 17th, 2008.
explore: Kitt Peak's Mayall 4-meter telescope captured this view on June 19th, 2009. In this view, north points left and east points down.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in orange and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: The nebula is so faint that it went unnoticed until 2008; narrow filters and a large telescope bring out its shell.

alt: A faint, nearly perfectly round shell of gas set within a wider haze of nebulosity and stars.

caption: The planetary nebula Sharpless 2-188, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A nearly circular nebula glows much more brightly along its lower-left side, while faint wisps trail away in the opposite direction. This is Sharpless 2-188, or Sh2-188, an unusual planetary nebula in the constellation Cassiopeia.

Planetary nebulae are shells of gas thrown off by stars late in their lives. Here, the expanding gas is crashing into the ambient gas of the interstellar medium, the thin material that fills the space between stars.

The lopsided brightness has a simple cause. The central star is moving rapidly towards the southeast, the lower left in this view, and that side of the nebula shines much more brightly as it pushes into the surrounding gas. Faint wisps of gas can also be traced on the opposite side.
explore: The picture was made to show off what the newly installed CCD detectors could do in the Mosaic 1.1 camera, which is mounted on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: Deep exposures with the Mosaic 1.1 camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in cyan.
understand.eye: Narrow filters and deep exposures reveal faint gas that the eye could not see.

alt: A nearly circular nebula, much brighter at lower left, with faint wisps extending towards the upper right.

caption: The Ghost of Jupiter (NGC 3242) and its surrounding gas, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Just above and to the right of the centre of this wide view is the bright planetary nebula NGC 3242, nicknamed the Ghost of Jupiter. Around it spreads a much larger, fainter cloud of gas.

A planetary nebula forms when a dying star casts off its outer layers, and the exposed hot core makes that gas glow. Close-up images usually focus on the bright nebula itself, but this wide field captures what lies around it.

The nature of that extended cloud is still unknown. One possibility is that it is a shell of gas thrown off by NGC 3242 earlier, when the star was a red giant. Another is that it is simply a nearby cloud of interstellar gas being lit up by the planetary nebula. Either way, the wide field reveals something a close-up would miss.
explore: Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope recorded the scene with its wide-field Mosaic camera on December 15th, 2006. North is to the left and east is down.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Oxygen [O III] is shown in blue and hydrogen-alpha in orange.
understand.eye: The surrounding cloud is far too faint for the eye; narrow filters and long exposures bring it out.

alt: A small bright nebula just above and right of centre, surrounded by a large, faint cloud of gas.

caption: The Elephant Trunk Nebula (IC 1396A), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This image focuses on IC 1396A, a dense, dark cloud of gas sitting inside a much larger glowing nebula. Its distinctive shape has earned it the informal name Elephant Trunk Nebula.

The larger nebula, IC 1396, is a giant emission nebula more than 3 degrees across on the sky. Its light comes from HD 206267, a hot and massive O-type star close to the nebula's centre. That star lies just beyond the top edge of this frame, so it does not appear here.

An emission nebula glows because intense light from hot stars energises its gas. Dense clouds like the Elephant Trunk resist that light for longer than the thinner gas around them, so they stand out as dark shapes silhouetted against the glow.
explore: The image comes from the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. North is to the right and east is up. The same gallery holds images of other parts of IC 1396.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, sulphur [S II] in blue and the I filter in orange.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and narrow filters isolate the faint glow of individual gases.

alt: A dark, dense cloud with a trunk-like shape set within glowing nebulosity.

caption: The Omega Nebula (M17), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: This wide view shows M17 in Sagittarius, a nebula with many informal names: it is called the Omega, the Swan and the Lobster Nebula, among others. It ranks among the biggest and brightest regions of star formation in our galaxy.

Being so large and bright, M17 was one of the earliest nebulae ever found, discovered back in 1745. Its hydrogen gas glows with a distinctive red colour, energised by hot, massive blue stars buried within the cloud.

Nebulae like this are stellar nurseries. When young, massive stars switch on, their intense ultraviolet light strips electrons from the surrounding hydrogen atoms. As the atoms recapture those electrons, they give off light at particular colours, which is why such clouds glow. The same stars also carve and sculpt the gas around them, shaping the nebula as it evolves.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in orange, oxygen [O III] in green and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters separate light from different gases and assign them colours, so the palette differs from what the eye would perceive.

alt: A large, bright nebula of glowing gas in a wide star field.

caption: The planetary nebula PuWe 1, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This wide-field image shows PuWe 1 in the constellation Lynx, one of the biggest and faintest planetary nebulae known. Despite the name, a planetary nebula has nothing to do with planets: the term dates from early telescopes, when some of these round glowing clouds looked a little like planetary discs.
PuWe 1 formed when a red giant star shed its outer layers as it neared its death. What remains of the star's core, a white dwarf, energises the expelled gas and makes it glow.

Its faintness comes from its size. As a planetary nebula expands, its gas moves further and further from the white dwarf that powers it, and it grows dimmer. Over time such nebulae spread out and fade, eventually mixing into the gas between the stars.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: The nebula is far too faint for the eye; narrow filters and long exposures on a large telescope bring it out.

alt: A large, faint nebula of glowing gas spread across a star field.

caption: The reflection nebula vdB 152 (Barnard 175), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A reflection nebula perches on top of a dark Bok globule in this image of vdB 152, also known as Barnard 175, in the constellation Cepheus. Thin red filaments run through the upper-right corner.

A reflection nebula shines by starlight scattered off dust, while a Bok globule is a dense, dark cloud of gas and dust that can hide forming stars. Embedded in the upper-right side of vdB 152 is the Herbig-Haro object HH 450, a jet shot out by a newly forming star.

Those red filaments in the corner are the remains of a supernova explosion. Whether that remnant will eventually crash into vdB 152 is not yet clear. The scene brings together the very start of a star's life, in the young jet, and the violent end of another, in the supernova debris.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in yellow and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and long exposures reveal faint dust and filaments.

alt: A glowing reflection nebula sits atop a dark cloud, with thin red filaments in the upper-right corner.

caption: The young star cluster Cep OB 3b, imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: Cep OB 3b is a rich, young star cluster in the northern constellation Cepheus. The brightest yellow star near the centre of this image is not a member: it is a foreground star that happens to sit between us and the cluster.
The cluster's own bright stars are young and massive. They heat the surrounding gas and dust and blow out hollow cavities in the cloud.

Around these heavyweights are thousands of smaller young stars. Some of them may be in the middle of forming planetary systems. Young stars are often born surrounded by discs of gas and dust, the material from which planets can eventually assemble, so a cluster like this is a natural laboratory for studying how stars and planets begin.
explore: Kitt Peak's 0.9 meter telescope supplied the four separate filtered exposures combined here. The image credit names T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage and T. Allen of the University of Toledo.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used four filters: blue shown as blue, visual as cyan, near-infrared as orange, and a hydrogen emission line as red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the hydrogen filter isolates the glow of heated gas.

alt: A young star cluster with a bright yellow star near the centre, among gas and dust hollowed out by cavities.

caption: The northeastern part of IC 1396, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows a small section of the northeastern part of IC 1396, a giant emission nebula in Cepheus that spans more than 3 degrees of sky. The slice seen here covers only about 5% of the whole nebula.
IC 1396 gets its glow from HD 206267, a hot and massive O-type star close to the nebula's centre. That star falls just outside the top edge of this frame, so it is not visible here.

An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that shines because intense ultraviolet light from nearby hot stars energises it. The gas then releases that energy as light at particular colours, with hydrogen and sulphur each giving off their own characteristic glow. Narrow filters that isolate those colours let astronomers see where each gas is shining and how the cloud is structured.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left. The same gallery holds images of other parts of IC 1396.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing structure the eye could not see.

alt: Glowing clouds of gas in a section of a large emission nebula.

caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-290, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: The bluish interior of Sh2-290 comes from energised oxygen atoms, and one side of the nebula is noticeably brighter than the rest. This is an ancient planetary nebula in the constellation Cancer.
A planetary nebula forms when a star of low mass throws off its outer layers as it dies. Sh2-290 is among the largest planetary nebulae known.

Its lopsided brightness has an explanation: on that side, the nebula is running into the thin interstellar gas around it, and the collision makes it glow more strongly. Old planetary nebulae like this one have had time to expand a long way, so their surroundings play a bigger part in shaping them. Different elements in the gas each glow at their own colours, which is how the oxygen in the interior can be picked out.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, sulphur [S II] in cyan and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters and long exposures reveal faint glowing gas that the eye could not see.

scaleExtra: Sh2-290 has a diameter of about 7 parsecs, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A large planetary nebula with a bluish interior and one side brighter than the other.

caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 134 and its blue arc, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: The brightest star below the centre of this image is WR 134, and in the upper left curves a blue arc of gas. WR 134 is a Wolf-Rayet star: a very hot, massive star that is shedding its outer layers.

Those layers stream away from the star at very high speeds. Part of the ejected material shows up as the blue arc, which formed where the star's outer layer slammed into the nebula already surrounding it.

Massive stars live fast and short lives, and they return large amounts of material to space. Structures like this arc show that process in action, as outflowing gas sweeps up and shapes the clouds that surround the star, long before it reaches the end of its life.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing an arc the eye could not see.

alt: A bright star below the centre, with a curved blue arc of gas in the upper left of a star field.

caption: The Crescent Nebula (NGC 6888), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: At the centre of this wide-field view shines the bright star WR 136, wrapped in the glowing shell of the Crescent Nebula, also known as NGC 6888. It lies in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan.

The nebula is a shell of gas energised by the powerful stellar wind blowing from WR 136. That star is a Wolf-Rayet star, one of a class of very hot, massive stars that are casting off their outer layers.

A stellar wind is a stream of particles flowing out from a star. In Wolf-Rayet stars it is especially intense, and it can sweep surrounding gas into a shell and make it glow. The Crescent is a striking example of a massive star reshaping its surroundings.
explore: The image was made with the NOAO Mosaic CCD camera on the National Science Foundation's 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The picture combines three emission-line images from the 0.9-meter telescope's Mosaic camera. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, oxygen [O III] in blue and sulphur [S II] in yellow.
understand.eye: Narrow filters separate the glow of different gases and assign them colours, so the view differs from what the eye would see.

alt: A glowing shell of gas surrounds a bright star at the centre of a star field.

caption: The planetary nebula HDW 3, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Hartl-Dengel-Weinberger 3, or HDW 3, is a large and ancient planetary nebula in the constellation Perseus, with a distinctive braided shape. The star that produced it is the faint bluish one just below and right of the bright star near the image centre.

A planetary nebula is the gas cast off by a dying star of modest mass. HDW 3's braids are thought to come from motion: as the nebula travels through the galaxy, it collides with the interstellar gas around it, and that collision twists and shapes the glowing material.

Older planetary nebulae like this one have expanded and thinned out, which makes them more easily reshaped by their surroundings. The bright star near the centre is not the source of the nebula; the true parent is its fainter neighbour.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: The nebula is too faint for the eye; narrow filters and long exposures reveal its braided structure.

alt: A faint, braided nebula with a bright star near the centre and a faint bluish star just below and to its right.

caption: The Pleiades (M45), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: Blue haze surrounds the brightest stars of the Pleiades, M45, an open star cluster in Taurus that is easy to see without a telescope. The cluster is dominated by several hot, luminous, massive stars.

That blue glow is not gas lit up from within. It is starlight, mostly blue, bouncing off dust grains in the interstellar gas that lies between us and the stars. Blue light scatters more readily than red, which is also part of the reason Earth's daytime sky is blue.
An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud. The Pleiades also go by other names. They are often called the Seven Sisters, and in Japan the cluster is called Subaru.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak, Arizona. In this view, north points right.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: The naked eye sees the cluster's bright stars, but the faint blue dust haze shows up only in long exposures; the I filter also records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A cluster of bright stars surrounded by blue haze.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 3628, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A large spiral galaxy seen edge-on stretches across this image, and a faint blue line reaches from it towards the upper-left corner. The galaxy is NGC 3628 in Leo, one of three galaxies known together as the Leo Triplet.
NGC 3628 is not quite the flat disc a spiral usually is. Its disc is warped, and that long, faint blue line is a tidal tail, a stream of stars and gas drawn out of the galaxy.

Both features are the result of gravity. Over time, the pull of the other two galaxies in the triplet has bent the disc and tugged material out into the tail. Galaxies that pass close to one another can reshape each other in this way, even without colliding directly, and faint tails like this one are often the clearest evidence of such encounters.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. The image is rotated 37 degrees clockwise from the standard north-up orientation.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The faint tidal tail is far too dim for the eye; long exposures on a large telescope reveal it, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a warped disc and a faint blue streak extending to the upper-left corner.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4395, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: NGC 4395, in the constellation Canes Venatici, is a spiral whose surface brightness is very low, meaning its light is spread thinly across its disc. Unlike most galaxies, its centre is small and faint rather than a bright, concentrated bulge.

Almost every galaxy is known to hold a supermassive black hole at its heart, and NGC 4395 is no exception. But its black hole is one of the smallest of its kind yet found, six times smaller than the one at the centre of our own Milky Way.

Small central black holes like this interest astronomers because they may help show how such objects grow and how they relate to the galaxies around them. A faint, diffuse galaxy with a modest core offers a very different case from the big, bright spirals that are more commonly studied.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: A galaxy this faint and diffuse would be almost impossible to see by eye; long exposures on a large telescope bring out its disc.

alt: A faint spiral galaxy with a small, dim centre.

caption: The planetary nebula HFG1, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A bluish bowshock curves ahead of this nebula while a red trail of gas stretches out behind it. This is HFG1, a planetary nebula in the constellation Cassiopeia.
HFG1 was produced by V664 Cas, a binary star system that is racing through our Galaxy. In this image the system is heading towards the upper right.

As the nebula ploughs through the interstellar medium, the thin gas between the stars, it builds up a bowshock at its front, much like the wave that forms at the bow of a moving boat. Behind, it leaves a red trail of gas in its wake. The result is a planetary nebula shaped not only by the dying star but also by its rapid journey through its surroundings, a reminder that these objects do not sit still.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the faint glow of hydrogen and oxygen, revealing a bowshock and trail the eye could not see.

alt: A nebula with a curved bluish bowshock towards the upper right and a red trail of gas extending behind it.

caption: The Flaming Star, AE Aurigae, and its nebula, imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter Telescope
story: The bright blue star at the centre of this image is AE Aurigae, in the constellation Auriga, the Charioteer. Around it, gas glows dramatically.
AE Aurigae is hot and massive, and it pours out enormous amounts of energy. That energy excites the surrounding gas and makes it shine, which is why the star is also nicknamed 'the flaming star'.

Hot, massive stars give off a lot of ultraviolet light, which can strip electrons from atoms in nearby gas. As the atoms settle back down, they release light at specific colours, and each element produces its own set. This image isolates the glow of hydrogen, oxygen and sulphur separately, then assigns each one a colour, so the result shows where the different gases are shining rather than what the eye would see.
explore: The NOAO Mosaic CCD camera captured it on Kitt Peak, mounted on the National Science Foundation's 0.9-meter telescope.

understand.summary: This false-colour image combines emission-line images from the 0.9-meter telescope's Mosaic camera. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in yellow, oxygen [O III] in violet and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to individual gases rather than matching natural colour, so the eye would not see the nebula this way.

alt: A bright blue star at the centre of glowing clouds of gas.

caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-68, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A patch of bluish gas surrounds a very blue star, while diffuse orange light spreads towards the upper right. This is Sh2-68 in Serpens Cauda, an ancient planetary nebula whose age is estimated at 45,000 years or more.
The very blue star at the centre of the bluish gas is the progenitor, the star whose outer layers formed the nebula. That bluish interior glows because of energised oxygen atoms.

The orange haze to the upper right has a different origin. It comes from the nebula's movement through the disc of our galaxy, as it runs into the gas along its path. Planetary nebulae usually fade and disperse over time, so one this old offers a look at a late stage in the life of these objects, when their surroundings shape them more and more.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points right.

understand.eye: Narrow filters and long exposures reveal faint glowing gas the eye could not see.
