caption: The ionisation front in the Pelican Nebula (IC 5070), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: Pillars of gas rise along a glowing boundary in this view of the Pelican Nebula, IC 5070, in the constellation Cygnus. The Pelican is a giant star-forming region close to us, and this image focuses on its 'ionisation front'.
An ionisation front is the edge where energetic light from hot stars is eating into a cloud of cold gas, stripping electrons from its atoms and making it glow.

Here, massive stars that formed recently inside the nebula pour out intense ultraviolet radiation. That radiation sculpts the cloud into pillars, eroding the thinner gas and leaving denser clumps standing. Because the Pelican is relatively nearby, it offers a close look at how newborn massive stars reshape the very cloud they grew from.
explore: The KPNO/WIYN 0.9m telescope captured the scene on May 24, 2002. It combines 7x6min exposures in hydrogen-alpha, 4x6min in oxygen and 5x6min in sulphur, and is rotated 135 degrees clockwise from the standard north-up orientation.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope used three narrowband filters. Oxygen [O III] is shown in blue, hydrogen-alpha in green and sulphur [S II] in red.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to individual gases rather than matching natural colour, and the faint glow requires long exposures.

alt: Pillars of gas rising along a glowing edge of a nebula.

caption: The galaxy trio NGC 5981, NGC 5982 and NGC 5985, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Three very different galaxies line up in this image in the constellation Draco. At the top is NGC 5981, seen edge-on; in the middle is the elliptical galaxy NGC 5982; and at the bottom is the spiral galaxy NGC 5985. Together they make a distinct trio.
An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of stars without spiral arms, while a spiral is a flat disc with arms. An edge-on spiral appears as a thin line because we see its disc side-on.

Whether, or when, these three will merge is not clear. But NGC 5982 already shows evidence that it has recently swallowed at least one smaller galaxy. Mergers are thought to play an important part in how galaxies grow and change shape over time.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: Three galaxies in a line: an edge-on galaxy at the top, an elliptical in the middle and a spiral at the bottom.

caption: The star-forming nebula Sh2-239, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Bright red knots and jets stand out in this view of Sh2-239, especially inside a cavity at the top centre of the image. Sh2-239 is a distinct nebula in the constellation Taurus where stars have been forming for quite a long time.
It holds two clusters of very young stars that are still deeply embedded in the cloud, along with many older, more evolved stars.

Those red knots and jets are outflows. Young stars often blast narrow jets of gas away from their poles as they grow, and where the jets slam into the surrounding cloud, the gas lights up. Seeing so many outflows here is a sign of an active nursery, with stars at different stages of development sharing the same neighbourhood.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter picks out glowing outflows, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A nebula with bright red knots and jets, particularly inside a cavity at the top centre.

caption: The emission nebula NGC 6820 and star cluster NGC 6823, imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter Telescope
story: At the centre of this image sits the open star cluster NGC 6823, wrapped in the diffuse glowing gas of the emission nebula NGC 6820. On the left, distinctive pillar shapes rise from the cloud. The pair lies in the constellation Vulpecula.

The cluster contains hot, massive stars, and their intense light is blowing the nebula's gas away. The pillars on the left are a product of that process: denser pockets of gas resist the onslaught longer than the thinner material around them, leaving columns standing.

An emission nebula glows because energetic light from hot stars excites its gas. Here the same stars that make the nebula shine are also slowly dismantling it, a pattern seen in many regions where massive stars have recently formed.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, oxygen [O III] in green and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters separate the glow of different gases and assign them colours, so the palette differs from what the eye would perceive.

alt: A star cluster at the centre of glowing gas, with pillar-shaped clouds on the left side.

caption: The reflection nebula vdB 24 and star XY Per, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Blue nebulosity near the centre of this image sits just above a bright star, and brownish gas surrounds it all. This is vdB 24, a reflection nebula in the constellation Perseus.

The bright star just below the blue glow is XY Per, a luminous variable star that lights up the nebula. A reflection nebula does not produce its own light; instead, its dust scatters the light of nearby stars. Blue light scatters most easily, which is why such nebulae usually look blue.

vdB 24 is set inside a much larger dark nebula called LDN 1442, which appears as the brownish gas all around it. Dark nebulae are dense clouds of gas and dust thick enough to block the light of stars behind them, so here a bright patch of reflected starlight is embedded within a dim, shadowy cloud.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint blue glow and brownish dust, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: A patch of blue nebulosity above a bright star near the centre, surrounded by brownish gas.

caption: The emission nebula Sh2-282, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Red hydrogen gas fills this view of Sh2-282, an HII emission nebula in the constellation Monoceros. Bright blue stars surround the gas, and several pillars are embedded within it.

An HII region is a cloud in which hydrogen atoms have had their electrons stripped away by energetic light. Here, the intense light of the bright blue stars energises the hydrogen and makes it glow red.

The pillars tell a story of erosion. Radiation and a strong wind of particles streaming from the brilliant blue star at upper left are sculpting them, wearing away thinner gas and leaving denser columns behind. Massive, hot stars shape their birth clouds in this way in many star-forming regions, and pillars like these are among the most recognisable signs of that process at work.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: Red glowing gas with embedded pillars, surrounded by bright blue stars, including one in the upper-left corner.

caption: The open star cluster M39 (NGC 7092), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
story: This picture shows M39, a loose and widely spaced open cluster of stars in the constellation Cygnus. By astronomical standards it is quite close to Earth.

An open cluster is a group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas, still travelling loosely as a family. M39 has around 30 members and is thought to be two to three hundred million years old.

Open clusters do not last forever. Over time, gravitational nudges from passing stars and clouds tend to pull their members apart, so the stars gradually drift away and join the general population of the galaxy. Studying clusters of known age like M39 helps astronomers compare how stars of different masses change as they grow older, because all the members started out at roughly the same time.
explore: The image combines 33 frames in B, V and R colours taken with the Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak's WIYN 0.9-meter telescope, outside Tucson, Arizona, during one night: September 15th, 2003. The camera uses eight separate CCD chips, so small shifts between exposures, called dithers, fill in the gaps between them.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera took visible-light frames through B, V and R filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The combined exposures record fainter stars than the eye could pick out, even through a telescope.

scaleExtra: M39 lies about 800 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A loose, widely spaced cluster of stars.

caption: The emission nebula Sh2-140, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows Sh2-140, an HII emission nebula in the constellation Cepheus. It sits on the southwest edge of a dark nebula called Lynds 1204, and also on the rim of the Cepheus Ring, a ring of molecular gas and dust.

An HII region is a cloud of hydrogen gas whose atoms have been stripped of their electrons by energetic starlight, which makes it glow. Dark nebulae, by contrast, are dense clouds of gas and dust that block the light behind them.

Hidden in the dark gas in the lower-left corner are about fifty young stars, deeply embedded and invisible in this picture. They cannot be seen in visible light because the surrounding dust absorbs it, which is one reason astronomers often turn to infrared observations to peer into such clouds.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Even with these filters, the dust hides the young stars in the lower-left corner; the I filter reaches near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A glowing nebula beside dark clouds of gas and dust, which fill the lower-left corner.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 286 (NGC 5560, NGC 5566 and NGC 5569), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Three gravitationally interacting galaxies make up Arp 286, in the constellation Virgo. The large spiral in the centre is NGC 5566. Below it and to the left lies the small, blue spiral NGC 5569, and at the top is NGC 5560, a spiral that has been pulled out of shape.
NGC 5560's distortion is presumably caused by the gravity of NGC 5569. When galaxies pass close to one another, their mutual pull can stretch, warp or twist their discs.

Galaxies that are close neighbours can pull material out of each other, bend their arms and sometimes trigger new star formation. Groups of neighbouring galaxies tugging on each other give astronomers a chance to watch, in a single snapshot, how gravity can reshape galaxies over time.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

caption: The bipolar nebula Outters 4 within Sh2-129, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A blue, two-lobed nebula is embedded in a vast red glow in this image in Cepheus. The blue structure is Outters 4, a bipolar nebula, and the red is Sh2-129, a giant HII emission nebula.

A bipolar nebula has two lobes extending in opposite directions, often shaped by outflows of gas. An HII region is a cloud of hydrogen whose atoms have been stripped of electrons by strong starlight, making it glow.

Outters 4 is named after Nicolas Outters, the amateur astronomer who discovered it, a reminder that amateurs still find new objects in the sky. Its origin remains open: it is not yet clear whether it is linked to HR 8119, the bright star at the centre of the image. Answering that question would help explain what created the lobes.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulphur [S II] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing a nebula the eye could not see.

alt: A blue, two-lobed nebula set within a large red glowing cloud, with a bright star at the centre.

caption: The northern part of Sh2-260, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows the northern part of Sh2-260, a puzzling HII region in the constellation Orion. The nebula has a twisted, double-lobed structure, and its second lobe lies below the area shown here.

An HII region is a cloud of hydrogen gas that glows because energetic light from hot stars has stripped electrons from its atoms. Such regions often take on complex shapes as radiation and stellar winds push against the surrounding gas.

What gives Sh2-260 its twisted, two-lobed form is unknown. One possibility is that it is connected to the giant lambda Orionis molecular region lying just to the east. Molecular clouds are cold, dense reservoirs of gas where stars can form, and a large neighbour could plausibly influence the nebula's shape, although this remains an open question.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A twisted lobe of glowing gas in a star field.

caption: The globular cluster M3 (NGC 5272), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Several hundred thousand stars crowd together in M3, a giant globular cluster in the constellation Canes Venatici. It is slightly larger and more distant than another well-known globular cluster, M13.
A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of stars held together by its own gravity. As in all globular clusters, the stars in M3 are old.

Photographing one is a challenge. The core is so bright that a single long exposure would wash it out, while the outer stars are much fainter. To avoid overexposing the centre, many short exposures were taken and combined. That approach lets the image show individual stars in the outskirts without the middle becoming a featureless blaze. Because their stars are so old, globular clusters are valued as relics from an early era of our galaxy.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: Many combined exposures record far more of the cluster's stars than the eye could pick out, and the I filter records near-infrared light.

alt: A dense, round ball of many stars with a bright core.

caption: The face-on spiral galaxy NGC 6946, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: We see NGC 6946 face-on in this image, its spiral arms spread out around the centre. The galaxy lies in the constellation Cygnus, and its activity is driven by brilliant, massive stars as they are born and die.

Those massive stars live short lives and end in supernova explosions. In the past century, eight supernovae have been seen in this galaxy's arms. That record makes NGC 6946 the most prolific galaxy for supernovae known over the last 100 years.

Spiral arms are where much of a galaxy's star formation happens. Massive stars form there, burn through their fuel quickly and explode, seeding the surrounding gas with new material that can go into future generations of stars. In NGC 6946 this cycle appears to be especially busy.
explore: The image was taken with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope on September 5th, 2008. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope observed in five filters. U is shown as violet, B as blue, V as green, I as orange and hydrogen-alpha as red.
understand.eye: The U and I filters record near-ultraviolet and near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the hydrogen-alpha filter highlights star-forming gas.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with arms spreading around its centre.

caption: The WLM dwarf galaxy, imaged by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows WLM, a dwarf galaxy in the Local Group, the family of galaxies that includes our Milky Way. It lies in the constellation Cetus.

Dwarf galaxies are small galaxies containing far fewer stars than large spirals such as the Milky Way. Because they are small and faint, the nearby ones in the Local Group are particularly valuable, since their individual stars can be studied in detail.

The picture was taken with the Mosaic II camera on the CTIO Blanco 4-m telescope as part of the Local Group Survey, a project sponsored by NOAO and led by Philip Massey of Lowell Observatory. The survey imaged galaxies through a set of broadband filters and also through filters tuned to specific glowing gases, and it made all of its data and measurements available through a public website.
explore: Beyond the broadband U, B, V, R and I filters, the survey also collected images through filters centred on emission lines from hydrogen (H-alpha), sulphur [S II] and oxygen [O III].

understand.summary: This is a true-colour combination of images taken through three of the survey's filters with the Mosaic II camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope. The packet does not say which three filters were used.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint for the unaided eye; a large telescope and long exposures reveal its stars.

alt: The WLM dwarf galaxy as recorded for the Local Group Survey.

caption: The spiral galaxies NGC 5905 and NGC 5908, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Two spiral galaxies share this view in the constellation Draco. In the upper-right corner, NGC 5905 faces us directly; in the lower left, NGC 5908 is turned edge-on. The two are relatively close to each other in space.

The contrast shows how much our viewing angle matters. A face-on spiral displays its arms like a pinwheel, while an edge-on spiral appears as a narrow band, often crossed by a lane of dust. NGC 5908 bears a striking resemblance to M104, the famous Sombrero Galaxy.

Scattered across the image are many bright, reddish stars. These have nothing to do with the two galaxies; they belong to our own Milky Way and simply lie in the foreground, between us and the distant galaxies.
explore: The KPNO Mayall 4-meter telescope captured the scene on April 10, 2007. In this view, north points up.

caption: The Cocoon Nebula (Sh2-82), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A small red glow sits inside a blue haze, and a long lane of dust cuts diagonally across the frame. This is Sh2-82 in the constellation Sagitta, which goes by two informal names: the Cocoon Nebula and the 'little Trifid Nebula'.

Sh2-82 is a fairly small emission nebula, the red part, surrounded by a blue reflection nebula. The two kinds of nebula shine for different reasons. An emission nebula glows because hot stars energise its gas, while a reflection nebula shines by starlight bouncing off dust grains, which scatter blue light most readily.

The dark diagonal dust lane hides most of the stars that lie beyond it, which is why the star field looks thinner along its path. Dust like this is common in star-forming regions of our galaxy, where it both hides and helps build new stars.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points right.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Long exposures bring out the faint red and blue glow, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A small red glowing nebula within a blue haze, with a long dark dust lane crossing the image diagonally.

caption: The emission nebula Sharpless 112, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Sharpless 112, an emission nebula in the constellation Cygnus, glows a deep red in this image. Its colour comes from hydrogen gas that has been energised by a star embedded within the nebula, known as BD +45 3216.
That star is far more massive than our Sun and gives off huge quantities of ultraviolet light. The ultraviolet light is what makes the surrounding gas shine.

Here is how the process works. Ultraviolet light carries enough energy to knock electrons off hydrogen atoms. When the atoms capture electrons again, they release light at particular wavelengths, and one of the strongest of these is a deep red line called hydrogen-alpha. That is why so many emission nebulae, including this one, look red in images that include a hydrogen-alpha filter.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points right.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A deep red glowing nebula in a star field.

caption: The central region of the Trifid Nebula (M20), imaged by Gemini North
story: This image looks into the central region of the Trifid Nebula, also known as M20, in the constellation Sagittarius. Gemini North, the 8-meter telescope on Mauna Kea on Hawaii's Big Island, recorded it.

A favourite of photographers, the Trifid is an active cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are being born. Among the massive stars at its centre, one is thought to have formed approximately 100,000 years ago, which is very young by the standards of stars.

Star-forming clouds like this collapse under gravity into dense clumps that ignite as stars. Once massive stars switch on, their light and winds begin to shape and clear the surrounding gas. Despite how often it is photographed, the nebula's distance from the Solar System is still debated.
explore: Estimates of the Trifid's distance range widely, which is a reminder of how difficult it can be to measure how far away objects in our own galaxy are.

understand.summary: The Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini North recorded this through g, r and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The z filter reaches into near-infrared light beyond the eye's range, and an 8-meter telescope collects far more light than the eye.

scaleExtra: The Trifid Nebula's distance is disputed but generally agreed to be somewhere between 2,200 and 9,000 light-years, according to Gemini Observatory.
alt: The central region of a nebula of gas and dust.

caption: The spiral galaxy IC 342, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: IC 342 is a spiral galaxy that we see face-on, in the constellation Camelopardalis, the Giraffe. Many nearby galaxies, such as the large spiral Andromeda (M31), appear tilted or edge-on from our viewpoint, but IC 342 presents its full disc to us.

That orientation makes it a prime target for astronomers who study how stars form and the chemistry of the gas between them. A face-on view lays out the whole disc at once, from the core to the outer arms.

Spiral galaxies are flattened discs of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind outwards from the centre. Much of their star formation happens along those arms, so being able to trace them clearly across the disc gives researchers a detailed map of where new stars are forming.
explore: The image was obtained in late 2006 using the Mayall 4-meter telescope and its 64-megapixel Mosaic-1 digital imager, and it was the subject of an NOAO press release.

understand.summary: The Mosaic-1 imager on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope recorded this through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see this way by eye; long exposures reveal its arms, and the I filter records near-infrared light.

scaleExtra: IC 342 is located roughly 11 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with arms spreading around its centre.

caption: The spiral galaxy M66, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: Bright blue and pink regions dot this view of M66, a distorted spiral galaxy in the constellation Leo. Those colourful patches mark places where stars are actively forming. The galaxy is estimated to lie about 35 million light-years from us.
M66 is being pulled on by two nearby neighbours, M65 and NGC 3628. Their gravity has warped the galaxy, and its arms appear to rise above the main disc.

Interactions like this can stir up the gas in a galaxy, and star-forming regions often glow blue from young, hot stars and pink from hydrogen gas lit up by them. A different trio of galaxies, around NGC 3190, lies farther away, so its members appear close enough together to fit within a single field of view.
explore: The image was made by Jeff Hapeman with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out the colours of its star-forming regions.

scaleExtra: M66 is estimated to be 35 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A distorted spiral galaxy dotted with bright blue and pink regions.

caption: Lynds' Dark Nebula 673, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: LDN 673 is part of a huge cloud of dust and gas in the constellation Aquila. In this image, parts of the dark cloud are lit up, especially in the upper-left and upper-right corners.
The cloud is broken into many fragments, and inside those pieces new stars are forming. Some of these young stars shine on the nearby dust and gas, which is what makes parts of the nebula glow.

A dark nebula is a cloud dense enough to block the light of stars behind it, so it looks like a shadow against the starry background. Such clouds are cold and full of dust, the kind of environment where gravity can pull material together into new stars. As the cloud breaks up, each fragment may give rise to its own stars.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in cyan, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint illuminated edges of the cloud, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: Fragmented dark clouds of dust against a star field, with illuminated patches in the upper-left and upper-right corners.

caption: The planetary nebula Abell 74, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Abell 74, in the constellation Vulpecula, is an ancient planetary nebula, and its age makes it a very faint target.
A planetary nebula is the shell of gas thrown off by a dying Sun-like star. Over time, the shell expands and thins out, and it grows dimmer as it spreads further from the star that lights it.

Old planetary nebulae are often bent out of shape, because as they drift through space they collide with the interstellar medium, the thin gas between the stars. Abell 74 is a surprise: in spite of its age, it is remarkably symmetric. That makes it an intriguing object, since it seems to have kept its shape where many others of its age have been distorted by their surroundings.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: The nebula is too faint for the eye; narrow filters and long exposures bring out its glow.

alt: A faint, symmetric nebula of glowing gas in a star field.

caption: The Wizard Nebula (NGC 7380), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: NGC 7380, nicknamed the Wizard Nebula, is an open star cluster in the constellation Cepheus that is still wrapped in the nebula it formed from.

The age of its stars is estimated at about 4 million years, which is young for stars. An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust, and in young clusters like this one, that parent cloud has not yet been cleared away.

Over time, the light and winds from the cluster's hottest stars are expected to erode and disperse the surrounding gas. For now, the glowing cloud and its newborn stars share the same space, offering a view of a cluster at an early stage of its life.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, oxygen [O III] in blue and sulphur [S II] in orange.
understand.eye: Narrow filters separate the glow of different gases and assign them colours, so the view differs from what the eye would see.

scaleExtra: The cluster is about 8000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A star cluster embedded in a cloud of glowing gas.

caption: The Dumbbell Nebula (M27), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Red filaments, a broader green glow and a faint blue outer region make up this false-colour view of the Dumbbell Nebula, M27 or NGC 6853, in the constellation Vulpecula. Its central blue star is only just visible.

The Dumbbell is a planetary nebula. Its central star is still ionising the gas around it, stripping electrons from atoms and making it glow. The name 'planetary nebula' is now a historical curiosity: astronomers now regard these nebulae as an ordinary phase in the lives of stars, when significant material is returned to interstellar space, and they have nothing to do with forming planets.
The nebula's distance and size are not known very accurately, because it is inherently very hard to measure how far away any planetary nebula is.
explore: The image combines two CCD frames taken at the Kitt Peak 4-meter telescope in 1988. Each was processed to correct for variations in the detector's sensitivity and to remove flaws from manufacturing defects and cosmic-ray hits.

understand.summary: The red structure is hydrogen-alpha light through a very narrow filter, the green is general continuum light through a broader filter, and the blue combines the two, processed to show fainter outer features.
understand.eye: This is a false-colour image, so its colours show different kinds of light rather than what the eye would see.

scaleExtra: The nebula is about 850 light-years away and 1.5 light-years across, according to NOIRLab, though both figures are uncertain.
alt: A planetary nebula with red filaments, a broad green glow and a faint blue outer region around a barely visible central star.

caption: The galaxy UGC 4640, imaged by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope for the DECam Legacy Survey
story: This image of the galaxy UGC 4640, in the constellation Hydra, comes from the DECam Legacy Survey, known as DECaLS. The survey was carried out with the Dark Energy Camera on the CTIO Blanco telescope.

It accompanied the survey's third data release, which made processed images and catalogues of sources available, spanning somewhere between 4000 and 8000 square degrees of the sky, in three wavelength bands. Anyone can explore the survey images using its online sky viewer.

DECaLS is one of three public surveys that together will image 14,000 square degrees of sky. Their purpose is to supply targets for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, a cosmology project at the Kitt Peak Mayall telescope. Large sky surveys like this record enormous numbers of galaxies, and individual objects such as UGC 4640 are captured along the way.

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope recorded this through g, r and z filters, spanning visible and near-infrared light. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The z band reaches into near-infrared light beyond the eye's range, and the survey camera records galaxies far too faint to see by eye.

alt: The galaxy UGC 4640 in a DECam Legacy Survey image.

caption: The Star Funnel (Sh2-126), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A yellowish dark nebula, nicknamed the 'star funnel', sits inside a larger cloud of warm hydrogen gas that glows red. This is Sh2-126 in the constellation Lacerta.

Dark nebulae are dense clouds of gas and dust that normally appear as shadows, blocking the light of stars behind them. This one looks yellowish instead, because several bright stars nearby are shining on it and lighting up its dust.

The red glow around the funnel comes from hydrogen gas. When hydrogen is energised by strong starlight, it gives off light at a deep red wavelength, which the hydrogen-alpha filter used here is designed to capture. The combination of a lit-up dark cloud and a glowing red backdrop shows two very different ways that gas and dust in our galaxy can become visible.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint lit dust and red glow, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A yellowish dark cloud embedded in a larger red glowing nebula.

caption: Part of the Monoceros R2 molecular cloud, imaged by the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: A bright red nebula glows just below the centre of this image, which shows a portion of the giant Monoceros R2 molecular cloud, in the constellation Monoceros.

Monoceros R2 is a site where massive stars are forming, especially in the area of that bright red nebula. A molecular cloud is a cold, dense reservoir of gas and dust, where gravity can pull material together into clumps that eventually ignite as stars.

Once massive stars form, their intense light energises the surrounding gas and makes it glow, which is why star-forming regions often stand out in red hydrogen light. Massive stars are relatively rare and short-lived, so places where they are being born are important for understanding how galaxies build up their stars and how those stars shape the clouds around them.
explore: The image was taken on January 11th, 2012 at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, using the Blanco 4-meter telescope's wide-field Mosaic II camera. In this view, north points right.

understand.summary: The Blanco 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic II camera used two narrowband filters. Sulphur [S II] is shown in blue and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the faint glow of individual gases, revealing structure the eye could not see.

alt: Clouds of gas with a bright red nebula just below the centre.

caption: The emission nebula Sh2-114, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Complex, wispy structures fill this view of Sh2-114, an unusual HII emission nebula in the constellation Cygnus.

An HII region is a cloud of hydrogen gas whose atoms have been stripped of electrons by the energetic light of hot stars, which makes the gas glow. Most are shaped by the stars that light them, but Sh2-114 has a particularly tangled appearance.

Its wispy form probably arises as winds blowing from hot, massive stars interact with magnetic fields in the interstellar medium, the thin gas between the stars. Beyond that, very little is known about this nebula. Magnetic fields cannot be seen directly, but they can guide the flow of charged gas, and in nebulae like this they may help explain why the glowing material forms such intricate strands. For now, Sh2-114 remains something of a puzzle.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing wispy structure the eye could not see.

alt: A complex, wispy nebula of glowing gas strands.

caption: The Cave Nebula (Sh2-155), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Sh2-155, informally known as the Cave Nebula, is a dark cloud of gas set within a giant emission nebula in the constellation Cepheus. The top edge of the cloud is lit up.

The illumination comes from several hot, massive stars of types O and B, which belong to a group called the Cepheus OB3 association. An OB association is a loose gathering of young, massive stars that formed around the same time.

Stars like these pour out intense light that energises the surrounding gas and makes the emission nebula glow. Where that light meets the edge of a dense, dark cloud, the boundary is brightly lit while the interior stays in shadow. Over time, such radiation can erode dense clouds, gradually reshaping them.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, sulphur [S II] in blue and I in orange.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint glowing gas, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A dark cloud embedded in a glowing nebula, with its top edge brightly lit.

caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 5363 and spiral galaxy NGC 5364, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Two very different galaxies occupy opposite corners of this image in the constellation Virgo. In the upper left is NGC 5363, an elliptical galaxy, and in the lower right is NGC 5364, a spiral.

An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of mostly older stars with little of the gas and dust needed to make new ones. A spiral galaxy, by contrast, is a flattened disc with arms that wind out from the centre, where much of its star formation takes place.

These two are likely in the early stages of a gravitational interaction. As galaxies draw closer, their mutual pull can distort their shapes and stir up gas. Pairs like this one give astronomers a chance to see how interactions begin, long before any dramatic merger.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. The image is rotated 15 degrees clockwise from an orientation with north to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: An elliptical galaxy in the upper-left corner and a spiral galaxy in the lower right.

caption: The Baby Eagle Nebula (LBN 777), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Brownish clouds fill this view of LBN 777, nicknamed the Baby Eagle Nebula. It forms one section of the Taurus Molecular Cloud, a vast complex of dust and gas.

The brown colour comes from large dust grains embedded in the gas. These grains reflect the light of stars inside and near the nebula, so what we see is starlight bounced off dust rather than glowing gas.

A molecular cloud is a cold, dense reservoir of gas and dust, the kind of place where new stars can form. Reflection nebulae like this one show where dust is present and lit by nearby stars. Clouds like the Taurus Molecular Cloud are important places for studying how young stars take shape inside their dusty birthplaces.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
understand.eye: The dusty cloud is too faint for the eye; long exposures reveal it, and the I filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: Brownish clouds of dust and gas lit by embedded and nearby stars.

caption: The Ghost Nebula (vdB 141), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Several stars are embedded in vdB 141, a reflection nebula in the constellation Cepheus, and their light gives it a ghoulish brown colour. It is sometimes called the Ghost Nebula.
Its less memorable official name comes from a catalogue. vdB 141 is its number in Sidney van den Bergh's list of reflection nebulae, published in 1966.

A reflection nebula does not glow on its own. Instead, clouds of dust scatter and reflect the light of nearby stars, so the nebula's colour depends on both the stars and the dust. Because the stars that light vdB 141 are embedded inside it, the dust is illuminated from within rather than from the side. The brownish tint seen here is a reminder that the colour of a reflection nebula is not always blue.
explore: The image was taken on August 28, 2009, with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points down.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope recorded this through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The nebula is too faint for the eye; long exposures reveal its dusty glow, and the I filter records near-infrared light.

alt: A brownish cloud of dust with several stars embedded in it.

caption: The emission nebula NGC 1491, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: NGC 1491, an emission nebula in the constellation Perseus, glows a deep red in this image.
The colour comes from hydrogen gas energised by hot, massive stars embedded within the nebula. Those stars pour out large amounts of ultraviolet light, and it is this light that makes the gas shine.

Ultraviolet light carries enough energy to knock electrons off hydrogen atoms. When the atoms recapture electrons, they emit light at particular wavelengths, and a strong red line called hydrogen-alpha dominates the glow. That is why emission nebulae so often appear red. Hot, massive stars are young, since they burn through their fuel quickly, so a glowing nebula like this generally signals a region where stars have formed recently. Their light and winds also gradually push the gas around, shaping the nebula over time.
explore: The picture was made with the wide-field Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points right.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A deep red glowing nebula in a star field.

caption: The open star cluster M7, imaged with a 16-inch telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This wide view shows Messier 7, also called Ptolemy's Cluster, an open star cluster in the constellation Scorpius. Under dark skies it is easy to find with the naked eye, and it makes a rewarding sight through binoculars or a telescope.
An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Globular clusters, by contrast, are dense, ancient balls of stars.

The open clusters we see are generally much closer to us than globular clusters, which tend to lie tens of thousands of light-years away. M7, by comparison, is only 980 light-years away, which helps explain why it is so easy to spot. Open clusters also tend to drift apart over time, as the gravity of the wider galaxy slowly pulls their members away.
explore: The image was made by Allan Cook with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a 16-inch RCOS telescope and CCD camera using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The cluster is visible to the naked eye, but a long camera exposure records many fainter background stars and their colours.

scaleExtra: M7 is only 980 light-years away and 25 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: The open star cluster M7 among surrounding stars.

caption: The Milky Way above the SOAR telescope, Cerro Pachón, Chile
story: The Milky Way's band spans the night sky over the SOAR telescope, which sits on Cerro Pachón, a mountain among the Andean foothills of Chile. Along the horizon, airglow adds vivid colours to the scene.

Airglow is a faint light given off by energised atoms in Earth's upper atmosphere. It is always present, but it is usually too dim to notice by eye, and cameras taking long exposures pick it up as bands of colour low in the sky.

Cerro Pachón hosts more than SOAR. Other facilities share the summit area: Gemini South, which forms half of the NSF NOIRLab-operated International Gemini Observatory, and Vera C. Rubin Observatory. High, dry mountaintops like this one are favoured for telescopes because they offer dark skies and a steady atmosphere, placing instruments above much of the air that blurs starlight.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera on Cerro Pachón, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and airglow appear brighter and more colourful than they would to someone standing there.

alt: The Milky Way stretches across the sky above a telescope dome on a mountain, with coloured airglow along the horizon.

caption: Stephan's Quintet, imaged by Gemini North
story: This Gemini North image shows Stephan's Quintet, a group of galaxies in the constellation Pegasus. It was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph.

The group is not quite what it seems. Most of its galaxies are interacting with one another, pulling on each other through gravity. But the galaxy NGC 7320, at the top centre, is thought by most astronomers to lie in the foreground, about 8 times closer to us than the others. If so, it only appears to belong to the group because it happens to line up with them on the sky.

NGC 7320 stands out here because of its many red blobs. These mark clouds of hydrogen gas where new stars are forming. When young, hot stars energise the hydrogen around them, it glows with a characteristic red light, making star-forming regions easy to pick out in images that include a hydrogen-alpha filter.

understand.summary: The Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North recorded this through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye; a large telescope and long exposures reveal them, and the hydrogen-alpha filter highlights star-forming clouds.

scaleExtra: The interacting members of Stephan's Quintet are almost 300 million light-years away, according to Gemini Observatory.
alt: A group of galaxies, with one at top centre dotted with many red blobs.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7552, imaged by Gemini South
story: This Gemini image shows NGC 7552, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Grus. It was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, GMOS.

A barred spiral is a disc galaxy with a straight band of stars running through its centre, from whose ends the spiral arms tend to begin. Bars can funnel gas towards a galaxy's centre, which is one reason astronomers find them interesting.

The target was chosen by a student. Benjamin Reynolds, then in 10th grade at Sutherland Shire Christian School, suggested NGC 7552 for Australia's 2011 Gemini School Astronomy Contest and won. Contests like this give students the chance to have one of the world's large telescopes point at an object of their choosing. The final picture was built from separate images taken through different filters, including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen gas.

understand.summary: GMOS on Gemini South recorded separate images through four filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, g in blue, r in green and i in yellow.
understand.eye: The i filter reaches toward near-infrared light, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates glowing gas, so the colours differ from a natural view.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 2158, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: This image shows NGC 2158, an open star cluster in the constellation Gemini, lying very close on the sky to another cluster, M35.

For an open cluster, NGC 2158 is quite old: its age is estimated at about one billion years. Open clusters are loose groups of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust, and most of them do not last very long.

Over time, gravitational tugs from passing stars and clouds in the galaxy tend to pull the members of an open cluster apart, so many disperse while still young. A cluster that has held together for about a billion years is therefore something of a survivor. Because all its stars formed at roughly the same time, an old cluster like this helps astronomers study how stars change as they age.
explore: The image was made by Neil Jacobstein with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures record far more of the cluster's faint stars than the eye could pick out, even through a telescope.

scaleExtra: NGC 2158 is located about 11,000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: The open star cluster NGC 2158 among surrounding stars.

caption: The lights of Andacollo at their normal level, seen from Cerro Tololo, Chile
story: This view from Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory looks towards the lights of the town of Andacollo in Chile. It shows the town's light pollution at its usual, everyday level.

The photograph was part of a comparison. During an event called Blackout for Our Skies, the lights of Andacollo were visibly reduced, and this image records how the town normally looks from the observatory.

Light pollution is artificial light that spills into the night sky, brightening it and washing out fainter stars. For observatories, even distant town lights can add a glow to the sky that makes faint objects harder to study. Events like this one help show how much of that glow comes from human lighting, and how much darker the sky can become when lights are dimmed.

understand.summary: This is a night-time landscape photograph taken with a camera from Cerro Tololo, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure can make town lights and sky glow appear brighter than they would to someone standing at the observatory.

alt: The lights of the town of Andacollo at night, seen from Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4654, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: This image shows NGC 4654, a spiral galaxy that the caption places in the constellation Coma Berenices.

A spiral galaxy is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind out from a brighter central region. The arms are typically where new stars form, while the central regions tend to be dominated by older stars. Our own Milky Way is a spiral galaxy too.

The light we see from a galaxy tens of millions of light-years away left it long ago, so an image like this shows the galaxy as it was when that light set out. Galaxies like this one also show how much a telescope can capture when a camera gathers light over long exposures.
explore: The image was made by Mitch and Michael Dye with Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, in 2014.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see in detail by eye; long camera exposures reveal its spiral structure.

scaleExtra: NGC 4654 is located about 55 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 4654.

caption: The polar ring galaxy NGC 2685, imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter Telescope
story: Unusual whorls, or helical filaments, wrap around the central spindle of NGC 2685, a polar ring galaxy found in Ursa Major. Other names for it are the Helix Galaxy or the Pancake Galaxy. The central body looks like a fairly normal S0 galaxy, a disc galaxy without prominent spiral arms.

What makes it strange is its ring of gas, stars and dust, which orbits in a plane almost at right angles to the galaxy's main disc. In effect, the galaxy has two separate systems of motion whose axes are perpendicular. Of all the galaxies in the Shapley-Ames catalogue, it was once described as the most unusual, and Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies lists it as entry 336.
The most popular explanation is that polar rings form through an interaction with another galaxy, possibly as far as a complete merger.
explore: NGC 2685 also shows weak optical emission lines but none in the infrared, which makes it an atypical member of a class of active galaxies known as LINERs. It is sometimes classified as SB0(pec).

understand.summary: This is a colour composite of CCD images from the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona, taken in November 1998. The packet does not list the filters or colour mapping.
understand.eye: The galaxy is too faint to see in this detail by eye; CCD exposures reveal its faint ring and filaments. The image spans 8.5 arcminutes.

alt: A galaxy with a central spindle-shaped body wrapped by faint, twisting filaments.

caption: The spiral galaxy IC 5332, imaged by Gemini South
story: Symmetric spiral arms unwind gracefully from a small, compact central bulge in this view of IC 5332, popularly called the Corsage Galaxy. Pink 'bubbles' dot the arms, and many smaller, more distant galaxies are scattered across the field.

IC 5332 has two main spiral arms, which keep splitting into finer, more feathery arms as they reach outwards. The pink bubbles are huge regions of glowing hydrogen gas, where stars are actively forming.

The crowd of galaxies around it is a coincidence. They are not companions but a chance alignment of far more distant galaxies, forming a backdrop from well beyond. Astronomers suspect IC 5332 belongs to the Sculptor group, one of the galaxy groups closest to our own Local Group.
explore: Isobelle Teljega, a student at St. Margaret's Anglican Girls School in Ascot, a Brisbane suburb in Queensland, Australia, suggested that Gemini South take this image. The suggestion formed her winning entry in the student category of Australia's 2013 Gemini Astronomy Imaging Contest.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Gemini South telescope. The packet does not list the instrument, filters or colour mapping.
understand.eye: The galaxy and its faint background companions are far too dim to see by eye; a large telescope collecting light over long exposures reveals them.

scaleExtra: The Sculptor group, to which IC 5332 is suspected to belong, lies about 10 million light-years away, according to Gemini Observatory.
alt: A spiral galaxy with symmetric, branching arms dotted with pink patches, surrounded by many small distant galaxies.
